newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel confident on 1997 growth, deficit goals.
newsitem.headline: Waigel confident on 1997 growth, deficit goals.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Friday he is confident Germany can reach 2.5-percent growth in 1997 and meet the Maastricht deficit target for participation in economic and monetary union (EMU).

Asked by Reuters about Germany's ability to meet its forecast of 2.5-percent growth, he said, "I am very confident. These are the figures that almost all economic research institutes have. I believe the fundamental data are good."
Waigel was interviewed outside a conference held by his Christian Social Union political party.

Earlier this week, the DIW research institute lowered its forecast for 1997 economic growth to 2.0 percent. But it is the only one of the six think tanks that play a key role in government policy-making to do so.

On Germany's ability to meet the EMU deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), Waigel said Germany had done everything it could in terms of budget consolidation, government austerity and transformation of the social system to meet this goal.
"I believe that under these conditions, our deficit will be under three percent," Waigel said.
According to government data released on Thursday, economic growth slowed to 1.4 percent in 1996 from 1.9 percent the year before. Its budget deficit was 3.9 percent of GDP.
Waigel was echoing the optimistic view put forward by Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Thursday after data showing unemployment had risen to a record 4.15 million in December.
"Chances for recovery rest on a solid basis," Kohl said. "Creating jobs is possible."
Underpinning prospects for economic recovery were low interest rates, price stability, a positive global outlook, a weaker mark and moderate wage settlements, Kohl said.
Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats, told German radio on Friday, "A growth turnaround is the absolute prerequisite for a change in the labour market.
"The growth turnaround has begun, and now the question is how (labour and management) use this change to create more jobs."
